input:
This study presents a detailed comparison of two catalyst forms for the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to produce dimethyl ether. The catalysts were assessed in terms of space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), along with pressure drop and activity loss. The experimental tests were carried out at a temperature of 280 °C and a pressure of 40 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3, and a single feed composition was employed throughout the programme of work.

The structured catalyst recorded a space-time yield of 0.7 kg L-1 h-1 together with a pressure drop of 0.22 bar, and its activity loss after 100 h was 8%. By comparison, the pellet catalyst achieved a space-time yield of only 0.31 kg L-1 h-1, while suffering a much larger pressure drop of 1.39 bar and an activity loss of 15% after 100 h. These findings clearly indicate that the structured catalyst is the superior performer across the full range of criteria examined, demonstrating considerably higher productivity combined with a substantially lower pressure drop and better retention of activity over the period tested.

It should nevertheless be noted that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in the course of this investigation, so the behaviour of either catalyst in the presence of sulfur remains unknown. In addition, yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature, which can make it difficult to place results of this kind in their proper context and only serves to emphasise the contribution that studies of this nature can make to the field.
target:
Two forms of a copper-zinc oxide catalyst for the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to dimethyl ether were compared on space-time yield, pressure drop and activity loss. Space-time yield denotes the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests ran at 280 °C and 40 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3 and one feed composition.

The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.7 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 0.22 bar, with an activity loss of 8% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave 0.31 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.39 bar, with an activity loss of 15% after 100 h. The structured form is ahead on all three measures at the stated conditions, and the margins are not marginal in kind: the yield ordering, the pressure-drop ordering and the activity ordering all point the same way, so the ranking does not depend on how the three measures are weighted against one another.

The ranking is bounded by the test basis. One feed composition was tested, no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and activity was followed only over the stated duration, so nothing in the comparison speaks to sulfur tolerance or to behaviour beyond it. A ranking stated on a wider basis would require the further tests that the comparison does not contain. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge; a comparison that reports both, for both forms, on the stated basis is the condition that allows the ranking to be made at all.
